content: The guidelines were established by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. New clinical and operational recommendations within these guidelines are derived using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which systematically reviews evidence and informs decision-making. These recommendations are further supported by modeling, expert consultations, and country case studies, which have contributed to the development of clinical, operational, and programmatic guidance. This process has also identified critical knowledge gaps that will shape future research priorities. In addition to the new recommendations based on the GRADE system, the guidelines consolidate existing recommendations from other WHO guidelines. Most of these prior recommendations were also developed using the GRADE system or a modified version of it, which assesses the strength of recommendations and the quality of evidence. The primary audience for these guidelines includes national HIV program managers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The guidelines are intended to inform country-level policy decisions and planning for scaling up antiretroviral therapy (ART). They also serve as a valuable resource for clinicians, development agencies, international organizations, non-governmental organizations, and other implementing partners over the coming years. The 2013 guidelines represent a significant step toward achieving universal access to antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV. They aim to enhance the efficiency, impact, and long-term sustainability of ART programs, ultimately contributing to the goal of ending the HIV epidemic. HIV Testing and Counseling Community-Based Testing: In generalized HIV epidemics, community-based HIV testing and counseling, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services, is recommended alongside provider-initiated testing and counseling (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). In all epidemic settings, community-based testing and counseling for key populations, with similar linkages, is also recommended (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Adolescents: HIV testing and counseling, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care, is recommended for adolescents from key populations in all settings (generalized, low, and concentrated epidemics) (strong recommendation, very-low-quality evidence). For all adolescents in generalized epidemics, this is also recommended (strong recommendation, very-low-quality evidence). In low and concentrated epidemics, it is suggested that testing and counseling be accessible to all adolescents (conditional recommendation, very-low-quality evidence). When to Start ART in People Living with HIV Adults and Adolescents: ART should be initiated in all individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or with a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). ART should also be started in individuals with a CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical stage (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). ART is recommended for all individuals with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count, in the following situations: Active tuberculosis (TB) disease (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection with severe chronic liver disease (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). HIV-positive partners in serodiscordant couples to reduce transmission (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women: All pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should initiate triple ART, maintained at least for the duration of mother-to-child transmission risk. Women meeting treatment eligibility criteria should continue lifelong ART (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). For programmatic reasons, particularly in generalized epidemics, all pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should initiate lifelong ART (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). In some countries, women not eligible for ART for their own health may stop ART after the transmission risk period ends (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Children: ART should be initiated in all children under five years of age with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 count. This includes: Infants diagnosed in the first year of life (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Children aged one to less than five years (conditional recommendation, very-low-quality evidence). Children aged five years and older with a CD4 count ≤ 500 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence for CD4 ≤ 350; conditional recommendation, very-low-quality evidence for CD4 between 350 and 500). ART should also be initiated in children with severe or advanced symptomatic disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4), regardless of age or CD4 count (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). What ARV Regimens to Start With Adults: First-line ART should consist of two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus a non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). The preferred regimen is TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + EFV as a fixed-dose combination (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). If this is contraindicated or unavailable, alternative regimens include AZT + 3TC + EFV, AZT + 3TC + NVP, or TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + NVP (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Countries should discontinue d4T use in first-line regimens due to its metabolic toxicities (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women: A once-daily fixed-dose combination of TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + EFV is recommended as first-line ART for pregnant and breastfeeding women, including those in the first trimester and women of childbearing age. This applies to both lifelong treatment and ART initiated for PMTCT and then stopped (strong recommendation, low-to-moderate-quality evidence). Children: For children younger than three years, an LPV/r-based regimen is recommended as first-line ART, regardless of NNRTI exposure (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). If LPV/r is not feasible, an NVP-based regimen should be used. For children three years and older, EFV is the preferred NNRTI for first-line treatment, with NVP as an alternative (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Monitoring ART Response and Diagnosing Treatment Failure All Populations: Viral load is the preferred monitoring approach to diagnose and confirm ART treatment failure (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). If viral load is not routinely available, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Second-Line ART Adults and Adolescents: Second-line ART should consist of two NRTIs plus a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI). The preferred NRTI backbone depends on the first-line regimen failure: After failure on TDF + 3TC (or FTC), use AZT + 3TC as the NRTI backbone. After failure on AZT or d4T + 3TC, use TDF + 3TC (or FTC) as the NRTI backbone. Heat-stable fixed-dose combinations of ATV/r and LPV/r are the preferred boosted PI options (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Children: After failure of a first-line NNRTI-based regimen, a boosted PI plus two NRTIs is recommended for second-line ART, with LPV/r as the preferred PI (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). For children younger than three years, adherence measures should be prioritized if first-line LPV/r-based regimens fail (conditional recommendation, very-low-quality evidence). Third-Line ART All Populations: National programs should develop policies for third-line ART (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence). Third-line regimens should include new drugs with minimal cross-resistance to previously used regimens.
